country.evidence_quote: The Yanomami is the largest semi-nomadic hunter–gatherer group of the Americas, exploring different niches of the Amazon rainforest in Brazil and Venezuela.
country.notes: Primary study cohort from Brazil; comparisons also include Venezuela.

body_site.evidence_quote: Participants were requested to provide a morning fecal sample, and a labeled screw-capped plastic container was provided.
body_site.section: Materials and Methods — Study Participants and Sample Collection
body_site.notes: Stool samples collected for microbiome analysis.

lifestyle.evidence_quote: The Yanomami group is mainly hunter–gatherers, but in some communities, the women cultivate plantains and cassava, while men go hunting.
lifestyle.section: Results — Lifestyle of the Human Group Studied
lifestyle.notes: Primary subsistence based on hunting, fishing, gathering, and swidden horticulture.

location.evidence_quote: They inhabit the Amazon region encompassing the Brazil and Venezuela border, living in villages located at sea level as well as on high mountains
location.notes: Participants from semi-isolated Yanomami communities in the Amazon.

westernized.evidence_quote: Human groups that still maintain traditional modes of subsistence (hunter–gatherers and rural agriculturalists) represent human groups non-impacted by urban-industrialized lifestyles
westernized.notes: Study explicitly characterizes Yanomami as maintaining traditional subsistence practices.

value: Study population: Yanomami semi-nomadic hunter-gatherers from Brazil (n=15) and Venezuela (n=8), plus Matses (n=24), Tunapuco (n=12), and US urban individuals (n=44)
Study design: comparative metagenomic analysis across traditional and urban-industrialized groups
Total reads generated: approximately 219 million reads with average of 14 million reads per sample
Taxonomic classification method: Kraken using NCBI whole genomes database
Functional classification method: SUPER-FOCUS based on SEED database gene families
Diversity measures: Shannon index (alpha-diversity), Bray-Curtis dissimilarity (beta-diversity)
Ethics approval: Oswaldo Cruz Foundation Ethics Committee No. 638/11 and CONEP No. 16907
Key finding: Yanomami/Brazil showed unique functional features including higher virulence-related genes for heavy metal resistance (cobalt, zinc, cadmium)
uncurated_metadata.evidence_quote: Based on shotgun metagenomic data, we characterized the gut microbiome of the Yanomami from Brazil and compared taxonomically and functionally with the Yanomami from Venezuela.
uncurated_metadata.notes: Comprehensive study metadata including participant demographics, sample collection, sequencing methods, bioinformatics approaches, and key findings.
